title: UN experts decry July surge in civilian casualties across Gaza and West Bank as humanitarian conditions continue to decline
content:
News

UN experts decry July surge in civilian casualties across Gaza and West Bank as humanitarian conditions continue to decline

UN experts on Monday decried the recent surge of violence and human rights abuses against civilians across Gaza and the Occupied West Bank, voicing concern that the rights crisis in the Palestinian territories continues to deteriorate at an accelerated rate, leaving civilians with no form of protection despite international appeals.

Fifteen UN experts stated that, despite the US-backed Gaza Peace Deal ceasefire, Israeli forces have killed about 160 Palestinians in Gaza in July alone.  The ceasefire was agreed by both Israel and Hamas and took effect in October 2025.

The experts were especially alarmed by reports of the killing of civilians—including women, children, and the elderly—who were sheltering in tents for safety. It is also reported that the killings took place in densely populated displacement zones which were far from the so-called yellow line. In early August, the UN expressed alarm around the reported installation of cement blocks around civilian shelter areas, further displacing civilian populations and expanding restricted areas.

The experts also noted alarming reports of the destruction of residential blocks and shelters by fighter jets and strikes on hospitals, stating that the killings of UN-contracted staff, humanitarian workers and human rights defenders are deplorable. Restrictions on movement have also resulted in deaths in the region. According to reports, a four-month old baby died and a pregnant woman experienced a miscarriage after ambulances were blocked at military gates.

The UN strongly condemned the “surge in settler terror,” citing an incident of settler violence near Nablus, where four Palestinian men were shot and killed, 80 residents detained, and buildings including mosques and homes reportedly vandalized and burned. Many countries have decried Israeli settler violence and imposed sanctions packages against supporters and financiers.

The experts called for immediate compliance with last year’s relevant International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion and international humanitarian law, including total and unequivocal respect for the ceasefire, cessation of attacks against civilians, and unimpeded humanitarian access.

International law, namely the Fourth Geneva Convention 1949, prohibits any targeted attacks and violence perpetuated against civilians and aid workers during armed conflict. Attacks on hospitals, schools, shelters, and civilian infrastructure is also prohibited. Article 15 of the Fourth Geneva Convention outlines that civilians must have safe, neutralized zones for shelter.

Palestinian militant group Hamas recently announced its dissolution of Gaza governance, in line with the terms proposed in the Gaza peace deal. However, the Israeli government’s latest announcement of its rejection of the peace plan’s terms—specifically, the disarmament of Hamas in exchange for full withdrawal of Israeli military—has drawn sharp condemnation. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has nonetheless affirmed this stance, stating that the Israeli Defense Forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed.

title: Minecraft finally has a Switch 2 release date, but there may be bad news for Switch 1 owners
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Means to an Enderman.

Minecraft on Switch 2 is a port that just makes sense. Everyone, including developer Mojang, agrees. On Wednesday, the developer officially confirmed a 27th October release date for the Switch 2 version.

Minecraft's Switch 2 port initially leaked through an ESRB rating back in June, before Nintendo confirmed it days later in a Direct showcase - though without offering a release date.

As part of this new announcement, Mojang mentioned a detail that may sour some on the news. While existing owners of the game on Switch 1 will be able to upgrade to the Switch 2 version, the upgrade does not appear to be free. The developer didn't reveal more besides, saying to expect more details to follow. This is becoming a trend for Switch 2 games; Nintendo itself expects paid upgrades for the likes of Zelda, Kirby, and Metroid Prime 4, whilst Square Enix sometimes skips the option of an upgrade path altogether.

The Switch 2 version of Minecraft includes a few visual enhancements. Mojang is calling it Vibrant Visuals, and it's essentially a bundle of visual upgrades like enhanced lighting and shadow effects.

Marketplace content does, for the most part, support Vibrant Visuals, which is great news if you have a library of mods. However, it won't be available with certain gameplay features, including when playing in split-screen and when using certain Marketplace Worlds and content. The Nintendo-exclusive Super Mario Mash-Up pack will benefit from the Vibrant Visuals upgrade, at least.

Minecraft's July preview build added craftable cushions for players to sit on, some 17 years after the game's initial release.

title: Much-wishlisted 100-player shooter Wardogs gets an early access release date, invites anyone unhappy with the closed beta to claim a refund
author: Sherif Saed
content:
"Here are 10 reasons you should NOT buy."

Wardogs, the ambitious shooter from Battalion 1944 and The Turing Test developer Bulkhead, will soon arrive on Steam early access. The studio announced today, after months of invite-only tests, Wardogs will finally be released on 10th September.

Pre-orders are live as of the time of this writing, and it guarantees access to Wardog's upcoming closed beta, which is available for one weekend: 21st-23rd August on Steam. And the developer appears to be so comfortable with what it's made that players are invited to request a refund from Steam after playing the beta if they don't like it.

The game is priced $40 during early access, but the plan is to raise that to $60 at full release. Early access won't include any in-game monetisation but Bulkhead said you should expect paid cosmetics after release. At early access launch, only the Supporters edition cosmetics will be available.

Wardogs matches take place in large open spaces that support up to 100 players. The game features Battlefield-style combined-arms combat, though with some of the logistical focus of Hell Let Loose, Squad or Arma.

Wardogs launches into early access with three maps that have three variations each, and several vehicles and weapons. Development in early access will focus on game performance, stability, balance, bug fixes and any other topic players raise after getting their hands on it. And the plan is to remain in early access for "roughly 24 months".

Bulkhead has taken a transparent approach to Wardogs' marketing since its reveal, with the developer regularly communicating its goals for the project with players. The studio has repeatedly said it's not making a game for everyone, and preemptively addressed topics it knows will be discussed - such as game performance versus visuals and the ever-controversial player count.

This continues today with a pre-order trailer titled "10 Reasons NOT to Buy". It's worth watching the video for an idea of what to expect from early access.

Control Zone is its main mode, where three rival teams of mercenaries try to capture key locations and secure cash. Said cash ties into the meta game component, which players use to buy weapons, vehicles and other useful items. The more successful jobs you do - even down to just transporting players around in a helicopter - the more money you make.

Through closed tests and developer diaries over the last several months, Wardogs has been building momentum, and currently has over 800,000 Wishlists on Steam.

title: If you drove yourself mad building computers in Minecraft, Pight's redstone-inspired puzzling is an affordable palate cleanser
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Piston/pistoff

If you're 1) in the mood for a soothing and affordable 2D block-shoving puzzler, and 2) have many memories of building frightful hydraulic slaughterhouses in Minecraft, then perhaps Pight is for you. Created by Turkish devs Mindlabor, it's about using pistons, dynamite, mystic portals, electricity blocks, and other cuboid fauna to move a lightbulb block onto a power source.

It takes open inspiration from Minecraft's redstone - an in-game substance that conducts power and thus, allows for the creation of preposterous industrial machines and even functional computers. The addition of redstone to Minecraft back in 2010 contributed to the rise of a whole genre of PC automation games. Playing Pight gives me a corresponding feeling of vertigo, though it's soon evaporated by the balmy straightforwardness of the puzzling – no need to worry about Endermen saboteurs in this one. Here's a trailer.

From the little I've played, Pight is very gentle. You click pistons to operate them, trying to find the correct order. There are 90 levels, with a new mechanic introduced every 10 levels or so. Later puzzles threaten to be "insufferably difficult", but there's unlimited Undo functionality if you snooker yourself. You can also build your own conundrums in an editor.

I don't write about Minecraft as a game, currently, because I'm participating in the BDS boycott, so it's nice to have a chance to apply my knowledge of Mojang's creation elsewhere. I have to say, this feels more like a love letter to Minecraft's pistons than redstone, though it could be that I just need to play on and unlock those electricity blocks. If you're interested, find it on Steam for the price of whatever £2.87/$3.19/€3.32 gets you in the Real World these days. A paperclip? Two acorns and a piece of string?

title: Halo: Campaign Evolved struggles to sell in anywhere near the quantities the recent Black Ops revivals did, and the probable reason? Lack of multiplayer
author: Sherif Saed
content:
A Master Chief Collection PS5 release "would certainly have done far better".

Halo: Campaign Evolved - the remake of the original Halo 1 campaign and the first Halo game released on PlayStation - has struggled to sell in meaningful quantities, and the probable reason for it? A lack of multiplayer.

According to Alinea Analytics, Halo: Campaign Evolved sold 1.2 million copies across Steam, PS5 and Xbox in two weeks. Xbox was the lead platform with 42 percent of sales - a figure that includes sales via Xbox app on PC - but PlayStation nearly equalled it with 41 percent, which left Steam with 17 percent.

The player number was higher because Halo: Campaign Evolved was a day-one Game Pass release, attracting around 2.1 million players on PC and console on the service, and approximately 600,000 of those spent $20 more on the Premium Pass so they could play the game five days early.

As for why the sales are weak for a ground-up remake of one of the most beloved shooters, Alinea analyst Rhys Elliott suggested the price ($50 / £50) may have been too high - especially considering the Master Chief Collection - which includes multiple Halo games and their multiplayer modes - is cheaper, at $40 / £40, and has dropped far lower in sales.

Alinea estimates Campaign Evolved brought in $67m (£49.6m) in gross revenue, a far cry from the recently released - and similarly Microsoft-published - Call of Duty: Black Ops 1 and 2 ports, which have reportedly brought in $435m (£322.2m) combined.

Elliott actually suggests it was those Black Ops ports that essentially stole Halo's thunder, in large part because they include multiplayer where Campaign Evolved does not. Despite being simple ports with plenty of technical shortcomings, the two Black Ops games outsold Halo 16-to-1, and it's all so players could relive their younger days in their multiplayer lobbies.

"The only thing the Halo remake left out is the one thing that turned two ancient COD ports into a half-billion-dollar phenomenon," said Elliott. "A Master Chief Collection release on PS5, multiplayer and all, would certainly have done far better than this campaign-only remake did."

It's a disappointing result for a game that, as the first Halo title released on PlayStation - a platform with a larger installed base than Xbox - probably could or should have had a larger impact. And it isn't because the remake is rubbish; quite the opposite. "Halo: Campaign Evolved is more successful at being a reinvention of an FPS classic than it is a reproduction - and that needn't be a bad thing," wrote Dom in our Halo: Campaign Evolved review.

title: "The world's becoming so bleak": How Soulframe hopes to escape Warframe's shadow, with a little insight from Elden Ring
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Fantasy RPG Soulframe's great advantage and possible curse is that it's from the studio behind Warframe, the free-to-play sci-fi bonanza that has kept chugging away since 2013, amid increasingly rocky prospects for live service games in general.

Warframe continues to pull a crowd, as was evident at this year's somewhat dystopian Tennocon expo, in which there was a whole auditorium set aside to house the queue for a bunch of T-shirt stands. That popularity gives Soulframe leeway to experiment and screw up, but it also creates temptation for developers Digital Extremes (who are owned by Tencent) to stick with what they know. Still, Warframe won't be a hit forever. As such, Soulframe's creators are trying to walk the line between lifting ideas from Warframe, and luring a new following with combat mechanics that take inspiration from Elden Ring.

According to Soulframe design director and former Warframe design director Scott McGregor, one thematic departure is that Soulframe's universe is relatively hopeful, however troubled. It takes place on a rustic medieval planet that is being colonised by a bunch of evil spacefaring moblins called the Ode, who are governed by a hypnotic Spellsong. As an Envoy empowered by a pact with ancient Fey spirits, you must stomp the Ode's raucous tinhat enforcers and free the moist-eyed critters they've imprisoned or corrupted. All of which reflects a conviction that the real world is going to hell.

"The world's becoming so bleak, and so hard to deal with, and everything seems to be getting so depressing," says McGregor. "And so when we were starting to work on Soulframe, it was looking for something that was maybe a little bit more inspirational, had a little bit more redemption to it than just, you know, more dark and evil.

"Those things exist in the game because you need to show the contrast and the evolution from that point, but for us as a team, it's looking for a happier place and a happier world," he continues. "And I think everyone feels that way right now. Like, the world doesn't feel like it's in a good spot, with the environment, with the political climate and all that sort of thing, so I think looking for an inspirational story or redemption arc is a big part of Soulframe."

Within that fuzzy objective of kindling optimism, the developers are also trying to peel themselves away from the sheer overkill of Warframe's combat. Soulframe has a bunch of projectile weaponry and ranged magic, but it hinges on methodical melee duels. It also doesn't have Warframe's absurd parkour system, which sees the most experienced players blinking through layouts in search of the choicest crafting materials.

"I would say we're still trying to sell that power fantasy to the player, but at a different pace and a different scale," McGregor continues. "Maybe you're a little bit more cosy, a little less bombastic. A lot of our review meetings, the stuff we talk about - we are trying to be very conscious about how explosive the screen is, and you know, how many times certain effects are applied to all of the enemies, or the number that you're engaging with at a single time, in a single fight. Making sure that it doesn't feel overwhelming for a single player, or a player who wants to play a little bit slower."

"I think what's interesting about working on this game from the design perspective is there's a higher skill barrier," he goes on. "Because it is a melee combat game, and there are some more timing-based aspects. You can get good at the game, even at a low level with bad gear and bad weapons. You could actually play at a pretty high level, if you have the mechanical skill… without necessarily having the gear."

McGregor draws a parallel with From Software's work. "You watch some of those Elden Ring players, where they go in there with a diaper on and the worst sword in the game, and they take on the best boss and you're, like, wow," he says. "Having it so that skill levels still matter, I think, is important as well. Warframe has a bit of that, but there's so much AOE room clearing - I'm gonna kill, like, 300 AIs with one button press."

Going by what I've played myself, I'm wary of Elden Ring parallels. Soulframe's melee combat isn't nearly as intricate or testing. Its open world is a sleepy golden expanse of forest glades and Ode camps in which you don't have to think too hard about terrain tactics, though there are some pleasantly enveloping dungeons beneath. Still, it's definitely more stately and precise than its older sister. It's a game of evasive rolls and parries in which you pay less attention to your stats. "It's definitely something that we're consciously always trying to manage," McGregor says, "and make sure that we don't go down that slope into Warframe land, because we definitely do want that contrast."

Like Warframe, Soulframe will live in 'eternal beta'. At the time of writing, the game has entered its 15th "prelude", these being the developer's Wordsworthian equivalents for early access updates. (Soulframe's writing in general is bardish to the point that I sometimes want to throw rotten eggs and tomatoes at it, like a drunken theatre goer in the 1500s). Digital Extremes are slowly adding stories, gear and areas while monitoring player feedback. After 13 years of Warfromage, the devs have learned a thing or two about keeping players glued to a work-in-progress, but they aren't, apparently, just reapplying the same lessons.

"I would say that there are some similarities, but the majority of the path that we're taking is actually quite different from the path we took with Warframe," says Sheldon Carter, studio president. "At least right now, that's what it feels like. One of the cool things, or also sometimes the chaotic things about live service is you're kind of driving the train while you're laying the tracks down." One rule of thumb is not to reveal things too early. Carter gives the example of Warframe's Duviri Paradox update, which was announced in 2019 and belatedly released in 2023. "We had to keep delaying it, because we didn't leave slack for getting punched in the face," Carter summarises, "and we got punched in the face on a few things between."

The major difference with Soulframe is that where early updates for Warframe were more about keeping the lights on, the new game has always been a live service project with a plan for years of significant changes. "I'll say the ambition is bigger on Soulframe from update to update, early in the game than we were on Warframe," McGregor recalls. "Warframe was a lot of really small, quick updates to add more life to the game, to add more content to the game. Soulframe updates so far have been bigger swings. We definitely feel like we've got to get back to those quicker ones, but there's an overall idea of what the story is, what the progression is going to be."

Soulframe's next serious update will add mounts to the game, together with a new pact that allows you to channel the Ode's grotty magic, and a quest about your Envoy's origins that features playable beavers. The most recent update, the aforesaid prelude 15, was more of an overhaul, introducing randomised weapon drops to address complaints about how long it takes to craft them. "Players can now get those weapons easier and try them out, but then, we also added the ability to sort of deeply invest into those weapons," says McGregor. "So, if you do find something you really like, then we added a crafting loop to go deeper with it."

Going by a quick read of the game's forums, players have mixed feelings about this latter update, with some protesting that their existing arsenals are now obsolete. As a business, Digital Extremes surely need to get this right, because Soulframe makes its money via the familiar option to purchase things you can otherwise grind for. As such, players need to feel that their time is well spent, but not so much that they can't be beguiled into coughing up for the occasional progression shortcut. In general, I'd love to get hold of some proper statistical analysis of how Soulframe's monetisation has been shaped by McGregor's desire to give players more opportunity to prevail, even when they're armed with rubbish gear.

Digital Extremes haven't released any real statistical info on Soulframe's players, but according to Sheldon Carter, the team's efforts to differentiate their creation from Warframe are bearing fruit. "There's definitely a huge segment of Soulframe that is a completely different type of player than those who play Warframe," he says. As for those who've come over from Warframe, Carter is fairly confident that they'll put up with a few blunders, as the game takes shape. "We don't take it for granted, but we've definitely earned [some trust] with our community, especially on Warframe - if we were to have a huge miss on something, they're going to be okay with us trying again."

This article is based on a trip to Tennocon 2026, for which the event's organisers covered travel and accommodation.

title: Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls patch swoops in to fix the game, improving performance for many PC players by lessening CPU load and stuttering
author: Connor Makar
content:
A quick 180.

Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls has struggled with some serious technical problems on PC ever since its release last week, resulting in a disparity between console owners and desktop diehards. Thankfully, a new patch seems to have swooped in to the rescue.

This patch, announced on the official Marvel Tōkon social media page and broken down at-length in the official Marvel Tōkon Discord server, attacks the most common performance problems players were experiencing. This includes micro-stutters, oddly high CPU use, and frame-rate drops.

According to the detailed patch breakdown, these CPU and performance issues were caused by "periodic audio processing" and "unnecessary" periodic checks of audio devices. There were also additional bug fixes including customisation settings being reset to default when the game restarted, and online lobby button input now being displayed properly.

The developers have also suggested two things PC players can do to further improve performance of the game on that platform. This includes warming up the in-game shaders and making use of the auto graphics via the in-game settings. That second one was a popular community fix prior to this patch, though the setting itself has also been improved..

So has this patch worked? Well, according to the reports of players on social media and the official Discord, it appears to have made a significant difference. One player - abhinav on X - wrote: "CPU usage slashed in half for most including me. Also played online a few games and got smooth games even in other regions as well now. But the netcode still seems worse compared to other games as of now."

Another player, FChampRyan on X, wrote: "Marvel Tōkon actually fixed the PC issues for most users. Unfortunately there's still some Potato PC's ruining the online experience. But overall this is such a fast turnaround."

As a result of this patch, some players are heading back to the game's Steam page to try and steer the platform's communal review score away from 'mixed' and towards something more positive. Steam Reviewer Rayden Belmont wrote: "If you're seeing negative reviews and wondering why, It launched in a near unplayable bad state. It remained that way for a few days, but as of August 10th, 2026, the performance issues have been fixed with a 10GB patch, so my vote goes back to Recommended. One of the best fighting games we've had."

title: CD Projekt cuts more than 20% of The Witcher spinoff development team 'to reflect the project's needs at this stage of development'
author: Andy Chalk
content:
CD Projekt has confirmed that nine employees working on The Witcher spinoff Project Sirius have been laid off, saying it has "adjusted the size of the Sirius team to reflect the project's needs at this stage of development."

"As a result, four people in Boston and five in Warsaw are leaving the company, while nine others have been invited to internal recruitment processes for potential roles on other CD Projekt Red projects," a rep said of the cuts, first reported by Kotaku.

It hasn't been a smooth ride for Project Sirius, which we first learned about in 2021 when CD Projekt acquired The Molasses Flood to work on an "ambitious project" based on one of CDPR's existing properties. The plan at the time was to keep The Molasses Flood operating as a distinct entity with its own "identity," but that fell to the wayside in 2025 when CD Projekt fully absorbed the studio into its own structure.

That move followed trouble with Sirius that ultimately led to a reboot and "updated direction" for the game. Five years after The Molasses Flood acquisition, we still know virtually nothing about the game—its proper title hasn't even been revealed yet.

And while the number of people being laid off is small compared to the massive cuts at companies like Xbox and Electronic Arts, 18 employees represents a significant chunk of the Sirius development team. CD Projekt said in its Q1 2026 financial report that 83 people were working on the game, meaning that more than 20% of the team has been cut.

title: "Expect fake messages": A load of Steam user personal info has been stolen thanks to a cyberattack on one of Valve's partners, claims report
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Seemingly, only Europeans are affected

If you live in Europe and have bought hardware from Steam in the past three months, then watch out, your personal information might have been stolen thanks to a cyberattack on one of Valve's shipping partners.

"Between July 29 2026 and August 1, 2026, a cyberattack hit CEVA Logistics, the company that ships Steam hardware to customers in Europe," reads a Valve email published by Gaming On Linux's Liam Squires-Hand, which has also been shared separately by Reddit users. "CEVA is still investigating this attack, but as Valve learned on August 7, certain information about Steam customers, including you, was likely compromised." CEVA have apparently "isolated the affected systems, taken all offline and brought in outside investigators".

According to the email, CEVA obtains delivery info from Valve, including your name, phone number, email, and postal address, when shipping Steam hardware to people in Europe. CEVA retain that info for up to 90 days after order. If you've been mailed about this by Valve, it doesn't mean your data has definitely been pinched: the email notes that Valve have decided to contact anybody "we can assume were impacted".

Seemingly, you don't need to worry about credit card information or nuking your Steam logins, as "CEVA does not have access to your payment information, passwords, Steam Guard codes or other information".

If you have fallen victim to the CEVA hack, you can look forward to a bunch of spam. "Expect fake messages - email, SMS or phone - that mention your hardware order and appear to come from Steam, Valve or a delivery company," the email reads. "They may quote your address back to you to prove they're genuine. They may ask you to confirm a delivery, pay a small customs or redelivery fee, or sign in somewhere to 'verify' your order. Treat all of them as fake."

The email notes that Steam Support never handle issues over email, Steam chat or Discord, so don't believe anybody who tries to hustle you on there. Also, don't click any links you get in suspect emails – type in the Steam store address yourself. And don't give anybody your password or Steam Guard code. All pretty standard safety malarkey.

The email promises that Valve are "pressing CEVA for the full scope of what was taken and how, and we are in the process of notifying the data protection authorities in the countries affected, including yours."

It seems unlikely, but not impossible that the email itself is a really tortured bluff on the part of some wily cyberburglars, designed to trick you into lowering your guard somehow. One can never be too careful, and I have duly sent Valve a request for clarification via channels I trust. I wrote all of it in capital letters to make sure they take me seriously. Whatever the truth of the matter, none of this is going to help sell Steam Machines.

title: Where to find the Shimanoyama region Treasure Hunt in Forza Horizon 6
author: Sean Martin
content:
The new summer Horizon Mascot Party Festival Series has arrived in Forza Horizon 6, and that means a new weekly Shimanoyama Treasure Hunt, plus more challenges and rewards. There are also two seasonal cars you can progress towards, the Exomotive Exocet Sport and the Datsun 2000 Roadster, and completing this challenge will give you a little bit of progress towards earning them. All that said, here's where to find the chest.

Forza Horizon 6 Shimanoyama region Treasure Hunt location

This week, the treasure chest is located at the Shimanoyama Drift Circuit in the far north-east of the Shimanoyama region. All you need to do to find it is:

  1. Head towards the circuit
  2. Turn off to your left and head under the sign towards the entrance
  3. Turn left into the circuit itself
  4. You'll spot a bunch of open garages on your left side with advertising banners on top—the chest is in the third garage along

Simply smash into it as usual and you'll get 100,000 credits, 5,000 XP, and 3 Season Progress points towards those two Summer Season cars.

For more progress, make sure to complete the photo challenge at Hokuryu Sunflower Farm, plus the weekly challenge involving the Toyota Japantakushi.
